units.title: Conductors, Insulators, and Semiconductors
units.tip: Electrical materials fall into three categories based on how easily electrons flow. Conductors allow current freely, insulators block it, and semiconductors can do either depending on conditions.

exercises.question: What is an electrical conductor?
exercises.answer: A material that allows electric current to flow easily
exercises.explain: Conductors have electrons that are loosely bound and can move freely through the material. Copper, aluminium, and silver are common conductors.
choices: A type of insulator
A material that blocks electric current completely
A device that measures electricity
A material that allows electric current to flow easily

exercises.question: What is an electrical insulator?
exercises.answer: A material that resists the flow of electric current
exercises.explain: Insulators have electrons tightly bound to atoms, making current flow very difficult. Rubber, glass, and plastic are good insulators.
choices: A material that allows current to flow easily
A type of conductor
A material that stores electrical charge
A material that resists the flow of electric current

exercises.question: What is a semiconductor?
exercises.answer: A material that can conduct or insulate depending on conditions like temperature and applied voltage
exercises.explain: Semiconductors like silicon and germanium have electrical properties between conductors and insulators. By adding impurities or applying voltage, you control their conductivity.
choices: A material that can conduct or insulate depending on conditions like temperature and applied voltage
A material that is always a conductor
A type of metal alloy
A material that is always an insulator

exercises.question: What determines how easily electrons flow through a material?
exercises.answer: How tightly electrons are bound to atoms
exercises.explain: Loosely bound electrons (like in copper) flow easily, making a conductor. Tightly bound electrons (like in rubber) resist flow, making an insulator.
choices: The size of the material
The colour of the material
The age of the material
How tightly electrons are bound to atoms

exercises.question: What is electrical resistance?
exercises.answer: The opposition to the flow of electric current through a material
exercises.explain: Resistance measures how much a material opposes current flow. Conductors have low resistance; insulators have high resistance. Resistance is measured in ohms.
choices: The speed at which electrons move
The opposition to the flow of electric current through a material
The amount of charge stored in a material
The number of atoms in a material

exercises.question: Why is silicon used in semiconductors?
exercises.answer: It is abundant, has good electrical properties, and forms a stable oxide insulator
exercises.explain: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, after oxygen. It forms silicon dioxide (SiO2), a stable, high-quality insulator that suits transistors.
choices: It is abundant, has good electrical properties, and forms a stable oxide insulator
It is the cheapest material available
It conducts better than copper
It is easier to mine than other semiconductors

exercises.question: What is the atomic number of silicon?
exercises.explain: Silicon (Si) has 14 protons and 14 electrons. It has 4 valence electrons in its outer shell, which makes it ideal for forming bonds in crystal structures.

exercises.question: What is germanium used for?
exercises.answer: A semiconductor for transistors and optical devices, though less common than silicon
exercises.explain: Germanium (Ge) is also a group IV semiconductor. It was used in early transistors but is less common today because silicon is cheaper and more stable.
choices: An insulator for protection
A semiconductor for transistors and optical devices, though less common than silicon
A conductor for wiring
A superconductor at low temperatures

exercises.question: How many valence electrons does silicon have?
exercises.explain: Silicon has 4 electrons in its outer (valence) shell. This allows it to form 4 covalent bonds with neighbouring atoms, creating a strong crystal lattice.

exercises.question: In a pure silicon crystal at room temperature, why is the conductivity low?
exercises.answer: All valence electrons are locked in covalent bonds, so few are free to move
exercises.explain: At room temperature, pure silicon's 4 valence electrons form covalent bonds with neighbours. There are few free electrons, so current cannot flow easily.
choices: Silicon is too cold at room temperature
Silicon naturally has very high resistance
Silicon atoms repel electrons
All valence electrons are locked in covalent bonds, so few are free to move

units.title: Energy Bands and Electron-Hole Pairs
units.tip: Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels. In a crystal, these merge into energy bands. An electron promoted above the band gap leaves a 'hole' that also acts as a charge carrier.

exercises.question: What is an energy band in a solid?
exercises.answer: A range of allowed energies for electrons in a crystal
exercises.explain: In an isolated atom, electrons occupy discrete levels. In a crystal with many atoms, these levels spread into broad bands of allowed energies.
choices: A single energy level for all electrons
A range of allowed energies for electrons in a crystal
The energy difference between atoms
The energy released when an electron moves

exercises.question: What is the valence band?
exercises.answer: The energy band occupied by valence electrons that participate in bonding
exercises.explain: The valence band is the filled (or partially filled) band containing valence electrons. These electrons are involved in chemical bonds.
choices: The energy band occupied by valence electrons that participate in bonding
The band where free electrons exist
The highest energy band
The band created by temperature

exercises.question: What is the conduction band?
exercises.answer: The energy band where free electrons can move and carry current
exercises.explain: The conduction band is empty (or partially empty) at low temperature. Electrons here are free to move and conduct current.
choices: The band that becomes full in conductors
The energy band where free electrons can move and carry current
The lowest energy band
The band occupied by valence electrons

exercises.question: What is the band gap?
exercises.answer: The energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band
exercises.explain: The band gap is the forbidden zone where no electron states exist. An electron must gain at least this much energy to jump from the valence to the conduction band.
choices: The energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band
The energy released by an electron moving
The width of one energy band
The space between atoms in a crystal

exercises.question: Why does silicon have intermediate conductivity compared to conductors and insulators?
exercises.answer: Its band gap is moderate, so thermal energy can excite electrons from valence to conduction band
exercises.explain: Silicon's band gap is about 1.1 eV. At room temperature, thermal energy can promote some electrons across the gap, giving it moderate conductivity.
choices: Silicon is not a true semiconductor
Silicon atoms are special and conduct electricity naturally
Electrons in silicon move faster than in other materials
Its band gap is moderate, so thermal energy can excite electrons from valence to conduction band

exercises.question: What is an electron-hole pair?
exercises.answer: A free electron in the conduction band and a missing electron (hole) in the valence band
exercises.explain: When an electron gains energy and jumps to the conduction band, it leaves behind an empty state in the valence band called a hole. Both can carry current.
choices: A free electron in the conduction band and a missing electron (hole) in the valence band
A neutron and a proton bonded together
Two atoms sharing electrons
Two electrons moving in the same direction

exercises.question: What is a hole in semiconductor physics?
exercises.answer: A missing electron in a covalent bond that acts as a positive charge carrier
exercises.explain: A hole is the absence of an electron. It behaves like a positive charge that can move through the crystal. Electrons can move into holes, making the hole move.
choices: A physical cavity in the crystal
A missing electron in a covalent bond that acts as a positive charge carrier
A defect in the material
An empty space between atoms

exercises.question: How does thermal energy create electron-hole pairs?
exercises.answer: Thermal vibrations give electrons enough energy to jump across the band gap
exercises.explain: Thermal energy causes atoms to vibrate. This energy can be transferred to electrons, promoting them across the band gap and creating electron-hole pairs.
choices: Heat removes electrons from the material
Heat melts the crystal structure
Thermal vibrations give electrons enough energy to jump across the band gap
Thermal energy reduces the band gap

exercises.question: How does a hole move through a crystal?
exercises.answer: When a nearby electron moves into the hole, the hole effectively moves in the opposite direction
exercises.explain: Electrons fill holes by moving into them. This makes the hole appear to move in the opposite direction. Hole motion is like the movement of a bubble through water.
choices: Holes are pushed by external forces
When a nearby electron moves into the hole, the hole effectively moves in the opposite direction
Holes do not move at all
Holes physically move through the material

exercises.question: Why can both electrons and holes carry current?
exercises.answer: Electrons and holes move in opposite directions, but their currents add up in the same direction
exercises.explain: Electrons (negative) move one way and holes (positive) move the other way, so their contributions to current point the same way and add together.
choices: Only electrons can carry current
Electrons and holes move in opposite directions, but their currents add up in the same direction
Only holes can carry current
Neither electrons nor holes carry current directly

units.title: Doping and the PN Junction
units.tip: Doping adds impurities to pure silicon to control its electrical properties. N-type doping adds free electrons; p-type adds holes. A PN junction where the two types meet is the basis for diodes and transistors.

exercises.question: What is doping in semiconductor physics?
exercises.answer: Adding trace amounts of impurity atoms to pure semiconductor to change its electrical properties
exercises.explain: Doping increases conductivity and allows control of electron and hole concentrations. A tiny amount of impurity, often parts per million or even fewer, dramatically changes the material.
choices: Coating the semiconductor surface
Adding trace amounts of impurity atoms to pure semiconductor to change its electrical properties
Heating the semiconductor
Applying electrical voltage

exercises.question: What is N-type doping?
exercises.answer: Adding donor atoms (like phosphorus) that contribute free electrons
exercises.explain: N-type (negative) doping uses donor atoms with 5 valence electrons. They form 4 bonds with silicon and have 1 extra electron that is easily freed.
choices: Creating holes in the crystal
Adding atoms with 3 valence electrons
Adding donor atoms (like phosphorus) that contribute free electrons
Removing electrons from silicon

exercises.question: What is P-type doping?
exercises.answer: Adding acceptor atoms (like boron) that create holes by accepting electrons
exercises.explain: P-type (positive) doping uses acceptor atoms with 3 valence electrons. They form 4 bonds with silicon but have a missing electron (hole) that accepts electrons.
choices: Adding acceptor atoms (like boron) that create holes by accepting electrons
Removing holes from silicon
Adding atoms with 5 valence electrons
Creating free electrons

exercises.question: What is a donor impurity?
exercises.answer: An atom that donates electrons to the conduction band
exercises.explain: Donor atoms (like phosphorus or arsenic) have 5 valence electrons. The extra electron is weakly bound and easily freed, contributing to n-type conductivity.
choices: An atom that blocks current flow
An atom used to create insulators
An atom that donates electrons to the conduction band
An atom that accepts electrons from the valence band

exercises.question: What is an acceptor impurity?
exercises.answer: An atom that accepts electrons from the valence band, creating holes
exercises.explain: Acceptor atoms (like boron or gallium) have 3 valence electrons. They form 4 bonds by accepting electrons from the valence band, creating holes.
choices: An atom that emits energy
An atom used in conductors
An atom that accepts electrons from the valence band, creating holes
An atom that donates electrons

exercises.question: What is a PN junction?
exercises.answer: The boundary between p-type and n-type semiconductor materials
exercises.explain: A PN junction is created by joining p-type (hole-rich) and n-type (electron-rich) materials. This interface forms the basis of diodes and transistors.
choices: The boundary between p-type and n-type semiconductor materials
A junction between silicon and another metal
A region with no doping
A connection between two wires

exercises.question: What happens at a PN junction in equilibrium (no applied voltage)?
exercises.answer: Electrons and holes diffuse across the junction and recombine, creating a depletion region
exercises.explain: Electrons diffuse from n-type to p-type; holes diffuse the opposite way. Recombination near the junction creates a depleted region with no mobile charges.
choices: Electrons and holes diffuse across the junction and recombine, creating a depletion region
Current flows continuously
No interaction occurs between the two sides
Electrons and holes move faster

exercises.question: What is the depletion region?
exercises.answer: A region near the PN junction depleted of mobile charge carriers
exercises.explain: Recombination removes free electrons and holes near the junction, leaving behind a region with only immobile positive and negative ions. This creates an electric field.
choices: A region near the PN junction depleted of mobile charge carriers
The edge of the crystal
The entire n-type region
The region where doping is strongest

exercises.question: What is the built-in potential (or barrier potential)?
exercises.answer: The voltage across the depletion region that opposes further diffusion
exercises.explain: The built-in potential arises from the depletion region's electric field. It opposes the diffusion of charges and is roughly 0.6 to 0.8 V for silicon junctions, depending on doping.
choices: An external voltage applied to the junction
The voltage across the depletion region that opposes further diffusion
The voltage needed to break down the material
The total voltage in the circuit

exercises.question: What happens when forward voltage is applied to a PN junction?
exercises.answer: The depletion region narrows and carriers can flow across the junction easily
exercises.explain: Forward bias reduces the built-in potential barrier. Electrons and holes can now cross the junction easily, allowing large current to flow.
choices: The depletion region narrows and carriers can flow across the junction easily
No change occurs
Current flows backwards
The depletion region widens

units.title: How Diodes Work
units.tip: A diode is a PN junction that allows current in one direction (forward bias) and blocks it in the other (reverse bias). This fundamental asymmetry is used for rectification and switching.

exercises.question: What is a diode?
exercises.answer: A semiconductor device with a PN junction that conducts in one direction and blocks in the other
exercises.explain: A diode is the simplest semiconductor device. It allows large current when forward-biased and blocks current when reverse-biased.
choices: A component that amplifies signals
A device that generates light
A semiconductor device with a PN junction that conducts in one direction and blocks in the other
A device that stores electrical charge

exercises.question: What is forward bias?
exercises.answer: Applying voltage to reduce the depletion region and allow current to flow
exercises.explain: Forward bias applies a positive voltage to the p-type side relative to n-type. This reduces the barrier and allows large currents.
choices: Applying voltage that widens the depletion region
Removing voltage from the junction
Applying voltage to reduce the depletion region and allow current to flow
A naturally occurring voltage

exercises.question: What is reverse bias?
exercises.answer: Applying voltage to widen the depletion region and block current
exercises.explain: Reverse bias applies a positive voltage to the n-type side relative to p-type. This widens the barrier and blocks most current.
choices: Removing all voltage from the device
Applying voltage to reduce the depletion region
Applying voltage to widen the depletion region and block current
The natural state of all diodes

exercises.question: What is reverse saturation current in a diode?
exercises.answer: A small leakage current that flows even when the diode is reverse-biased
exercises.explain: Even when reverse-biased, thermal generation of electron-hole pairs creates a small current. This is the reverse saturation current, which is usually very small.
choices: A small leakage current that flows even when the diode is reverse-biased
Current created by external sources
The maximum current a diode can conduct
Current that flows only in forward direction

exercises.question: What is the I-V characteristic of a diode?
exercises.answer: A curve showing exponential current increase with forward voltage and small reverse leakage
exercises.explain: The I-V curve shows exponential increase in forward current above the threshold voltage, and nearly zero current in reverse until breakdown occurs.
choices: A random pattern with no meaning
A curve showing exponential current increase with forward voltage and small reverse leakage
A straight line indicating constant resistance
A horizontal line at constant current

exercises.question: What is rectification?
exercises.answer: Converting AC current to DC by allowing current in only one direction
exercises.explain: A diode rectifies AC to DC by conducting on positive half-cycles and blocking on negative. Multiple diodes in a bridge rectifier improve efficiency.
choices: Removing noise from a signal
Increasing the voltage of a source
Converting AC current to DC by allowing current in only one direction
Making an electrical signal stronger

exercises.question: What is avalanche breakdown in a reverse-biased diode?
exercises.answer: A rapid increase in current when reverse voltage exceeds a critical value
exercises.explain: At high reverse voltage, the electric field is strong enough to accelerate carriers into ionisation, creating more carriers in a runaway process.
choices: A slow, controlled increase in reverse current
A rapid increase in current when reverse voltage exceeds a critical value
A heating effect in the diode
The normal operation of a diode

exercises.question: What is the breakdown voltage of a diode?
exercises.answer: The reverse voltage at which the reverse current rises sharply
exercises.explain: The breakdown voltage is the reverse voltage at which the reverse current rises sharply. It varies by design and doping level, and ordinary diodes can be damaged if the current is not limited.
choices: The maximum current the diode can handle
The temperature at which the diode fails
The reverse voltage at which the reverse current rises sharply
The forward voltage needed to conduct current

exercises.question: What is a Zener diode?
exercises.answer: A heavily doped diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown for voltage regulation
exercises.explain: A Zener diode is deliberately designed to break down at a specific voltage. It maintains a nearly constant voltage across it, making it useful for voltage regulation.
choices: A high-frequency diode
A diode that conducts in both directions
A diode optimised for forward conduction
A heavily doped diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown for voltage regulation

exercises.question: What is a photodiode?
exercises.answer: A diode that generates current when light hits the junction
exercises.explain: A photodiode converts light into electrical current. The photons excite electron-hole pairs at the junction, creating photocurrent.
choices: A diode used only in dark environments
A diode that emits light
A diode that generates current when light hits the junction
A diode that measures temperature

units.title: How MOSFETs Work
units.tip: A MOSFET is a transistor controlled by voltage applied to an insulated gate. The gate voltage modulates a conducting channel between source and drain, allowing current control.

exercises.question: What does MOSFET stand for?
exercises.answer: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
exercises.explain: A MOSFET has a metal (or poly-Si) gate separated from the semiconductor by an insulating oxide layer, typically silicon dioxide.
choices: Metal-Operated Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
Multiple Operating System Field-Effect Transistor
Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
Modulated Output Switch Field-Effect Transistor

exercises.question: What is the gate in a MOSFET?
exercises.answer: An insulated electrode that creates an electric field to control current flow
exercises.explain: The gate is a metal or poly-Si electrode separated from the semiconductor by oxide. Voltage on the gate creates an electric field that modulates the channel.
choices: An insulated electrode that creates an electric field to control current flow
A heat sink
The source of electrons
A physical opening in the transistor

exercises.question: What is the channel in a MOSFET?
exercises.answer: The region of semiconductor between source and drain where current flows
exercises.explain: The channel is the conducting path created by the gate's electric field. The gate voltage controls whether the channel conducts strongly or weakly.
choices: The oxide insulator
The metal gate
The region of semiconductor between source and drain where current flows
The substrate material

exercises.question: What is threshold voltage (Vth)?
exercises.answer: The gate voltage at which the channel just begins to conduct
exercises.explain: Threshold voltage is the minimum gate voltage needed to create a conductive channel. Below Vth, no channel forms and only a tiny leakage current flows.
choices: The gate voltage that destroys the transistor
The voltage that reverse-biases the junction
The voltage between source and drain
The gate voltage at which the channel just begins to conduct

exercises.question: What is the difference between n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs?
exercises.answer: N-channel uses electrons as carriers; p-channel uses holes, so their polarities are opposite
exercises.explain: In n-channel, applying positive gate voltage attracts electrons to form the channel. In p-channel, negative gate voltage attracts holes. Both can be used in complementary pairs.
choices: N-channel is faster
P-channel is stronger
There is no practical difference
N-channel uses electrons as carriers; p-channel uses holes, so their polarities are opposite

exercises.question: What is the cutoff region in MOSFET operation?
exercises.answer: When gate voltage is below threshold and no current flows
exercises.explain: In cutoff (off state), the gate voltage is insufficient to create a conducting channel. The transistor blocks current.
choices: When gate voltage is below threshold and no current flows
When the transistor is conducting maximum current
When the gate voltage is very high
When the channel is pinched off by drain voltage

exercises.question: What is the triode (linear) region?
exercises.answer: When gate voltage exceeds threshold and drain voltage is low, so resistance is controlled by gate
exercises.explain: In the triode region, the channel is conducting and its resistance varies with gate voltage, so the MOSFET acts like a voltage-controlled resistor. It is also the usual on state of a switch.
choices: When source and drain are shorted
When the transistor is turned off
When gate voltage exceeds threshold and drain voltage is low, so resistance is controlled by gate
When the transistor reaches breakdown

exercises.question: What is the saturation region?
exercises.answer: When gate voltage exceeds threshold and drain voltage is high, so current is nearly independent of drain voltage
exercises.explain: In saturation, increasing drain voltage does not increase current much. The current depends mainly on gate voltage, making this region useful for amplification.
choices: When the transistor is physically flooded with charge
When the transistor is off
When gate voltage exceeds threshold and drain voltage is high, so current is nearly independent of drain voltage
When current reaches zero

exercises.question: How is a MOSFET used as a switch?
exercises.answer: By toggling between cutoff (off) and triode (on) with gate voltage
exercises.explain: In switching, the gate voltage is driven below and above threshold. The transistor toggles between nearly zero current (off, cutoff) and a low-resistance conducting state (on, triode).
choices: By applying AC to the source
By changing the substrate voltage
By modulating the drain voltage
By toggling between cutoff (off) and triode (on) with gate voltage

exercises.question: Why are MOSFETs the dominant transistor technology in modern chips?
exercises.answer: They are simple, small, consume little power, and switch very fast
exercises.explain: MOSFETs can be scaled to nanometre dimensions, use very little power when idle, and switch in a fraction of a nanosecond. Billions fit on a single chip.
choices: They work at very high voltages
They were invented first
They need no power supply to operate
They are simple, small, consume little power, and switch very fast

units.title: Integrated Circuits
units.tip: Integrated circuits pack millions or billions of transistors on one chip. MOSFETs are fabricated in lithographic layers. The same physics scales from discrete diodes to advanced processors.

exercises.question: What is an integrated circuit (IC)?
exercises.answer: Multiple transistors, diodes, and other components fabricated on a single semiconductor chip
exercises.explain: An IC combines thousands to billions of components on one piece of silicon. This enables complex circuits at low cost.
choices: A single transistor with multiple leads
A circuit made of discrete components connected by wires
Multiple transistors, diodes, and other components fabricated on a single semiconductor chip
A component used only in amplifiers

exercises.question: What is photolithography in chip fabrication?
exercises.answer: Using light through a mask to define circuit patterns on a wafer
exercises.explain: Photolithography is the primary technique for patterning circuits. Light is shone through a mask onto photoresist-coated silicon, defining small features.
choices: A technique for measuring chip size
Using light through a mask to define circuit patterns on a wafer
A method for cooling chips
A way to add colour to chips

exercises.question: What is a feature size in chip manufacturing?
exercises.answer: The smallest dimension of transistors and connections that can be fabricated
exercises.explain: Feature size refers to the smallest dimensions that can be made, such as gate length and minimum spacing. Modern node names are mostly marketing labels, but smaller features still allow more transistors and faster switching.
choices: The size of the entire chip
The thickness of the silicon wafer
The number of layers in the chip
The smallest dimension of transistors and connections that can be fabricated

exercises.question: What does it mean to scale down transistors?
exercises.answer: Making transistors smaller and packing more onto the same area
exercises.explain: Scaling reduces feature size. Smaller transistors switch faster, consume less power, and more fit on a chip, following Moore's Law trends.
choices: Reducing the number of transistors on a chip
Making transistors smaller and packing more onto the same area
Changing the material from silicon to germanium
Increasing the size of transistors

exercises.question: What is a wafer in semiconductor fabrication?
exercises.answer: A thin, circular slice of silicon on which multiple chips are fabricated
exercises.explain: A wafer is typically 300mm in diameter and a fraction of a millimetre thick. Hundreds of chips are made on a single wafer, then separated.
choices: A protective coating on chips
A single transistor
A tool used in manufacturing
A thin, circular slice of silicon on which multiple chips are fabricated

exercises.question: How is a CMOS inverter (NOT gate) built?
exercises.answer: Using complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs that are always in opposite states
exercises.explain: A CMOS inverter uses one n-channel and one p-channel MOSFET. When one is on, the other is off. This provides fast switching with minimal power.
choices: Using only n-channel MOSFETs
Using complementary n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs that are always in opposite states
Using two resistors and a transistor
Using diodes and resistors

exercises.question: What is CMOS technology?
exercises.answer: Complementary MOS, using both n-channel and p-channel transistors for low power consumption
exercises.explain: CMOS uses complementary transistor pairs that draw power only during switching. This makes it much more power-efficient than older NMOS technology.
choices: Complementary MOS, using both n-channel and p-channel transistors for low power consumption
Conducting Metal Operating System
A type of memory technology
A single type of MOSFET

exercises.question: Why are computer logic circuits built as digital on/off circuits rather than analogue ones?
exercises.answer: Binary (on/off) operation is more robust to noise and easier to design at large scale
exercises.explain: Digital circuits use transistors as switches (on/off), not amplifiers. This makes them less sensitive to parameter variations and noise.
choices: Digital circuits are always faster
Binary (on/off) operation is more robust to noise and easier to design at large scale
Analogue circuits use different components entirely
MOSFETs cannot amplify analogue signals

exercises.question: What is a logic gate?
exercises.answer: A circuit built from transistors that performs Boolean operations on binary inputs
exercises.explain: Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT) are built from MOSFETs. They take binary inputs and produce a binary output according to a logical function.
choices: A physical gate in the manufacturing process
A type of diode
A component used only in power supplies
A circuit built from transistors that performs Boolean operations on binary inputs

exercises.question: How do processors scale to billions of transistors without overheating?
exercises.answer: Using efficient CMOS switching, clock gating, and thermal management techniques
exercises.explain: Modern processors use low-power designs, turn off unused circuits, and dissipate heat through heat sinks. Each transistor draws little power, so billions can fit.
choices: Transistors do not generate heat
Using efficient CMOS switching, clock gating, and thermal management techniques
By reducing the supply voltage to zero
Large processors inherently cannot scale further
